dailyBrief.text: Solon starts clear and chilly at 38°, but Sunday turns sunny and dry with a high near 68° and no rain — a beautiful fall day. Overnight, the Cavs won their home opener 125-121 over Brooklyn after nearly blowing a 22-point lead, and the Brewers rallied from 4-0 down to beat the Rays 5-4 and take a 2-0 World Series lead. The big national story is mixed signals on Iran — a U.S. envoy said a strike could come this weekend while President Trump played it down — and in France, a second weekend of cost-of-living protests ended with nearly 1,000 arrests. Today at home: the Browns (4-2) play at Tennessee at 1 PM on CBS with Sampson and Delpit back, and the North Union Farmers Market holds its season finale in Chagrin Falls from 9 AM to noon. One voting note: there is no early in-person voting in Ohio today — it resumes Monday with longer hours.

weekBrief.text: The week ahead in Solon stays dry and mild for late October: mostly sunny, highs in the upper 60s to low 70s, lows in the 40s and 50s, and no real rain chance until next Sunday. It is a full sports week — the Cavs are home against Minnesota on Monday, World Series Game 3 is Monday in St. Petersburg with Milwaukee up 2-0, and Ohio State travels to USC on Saturday night, Halloween, still sorting out its quarterback situation with Julian Sayin out. It is also the final full week of early voting in Ohio: hours expand Monday, mail-ballot requests are due Tuesday by 8:30 PM, and more than 920,000 Ohioans have already voted. The standout deal remains Miles Farmers Market's jumbo eggs at $1.00 a dozen through Tuesday. And with the baby due in early November, this is the last full week for finishing touches — and for getting out to enjoy the fall weather while it lasts.

Serbia's Vučić concedes defeat as student-led movement wins parliament
items.summary:
Serbia's Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat on Sunday night in a snap parliamentary election, saying the student-backed opposition list had beaten his Serbian Progressive Party after 14 years in power. Speaking at party headquarters, Vučić said a stratified sample showed the Students' List taking roughly 135 to 140 of the 250 seats in the National Assembly, against about 105 for his list — comfortably past the 126 needed for a majority. An independent Ipsos/CeSID projection pointed the same way, putting the students near 52 percent of the vote.

The snap election, which Vučić called in September, capped almost two years of student-led demonstrations. The protests began after a train station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in 2024, killing 16 people, and grew into a broad movement against corruption and creeping authoritarianism. The students became the most serious challenge Vučić has faced since he first became prime minister in 2014 and then president in 2017.

The concession is a seismic shift for Serbia and for the Balkans. A parliament led by a protest movement with no traditional party machine will have to turn street momentum into governing — forming a cabinet, setting a budget and deciding how far to push institutional reforms. Vučić's own next role is also an open question after more than a decade at the center of Serbian politics.

The official count from the Republic Electoral Commission is still coming in, and the earliest partial tallies were not representative of the final picture. Watch for the certified seat totals, the first statements from the Students' List about forming a government, and reactions from the EU and neighboring capitals.

items.title: Brazil runoff count begins with Lula ahead in the first returns
items.summary:
Brazilians voted Sunday in a presidential runoff between President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 81, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, and the first returns pointed Lula's way. With only about 0.3 percent of polls reported in the live count, Lula held about 57.7 percent to Bolsonaro's 42.3 percent — an early slice of the vote that is not yet a projection and could move substantially as more machines report.

Bolsonaro won the October 4 first round with about 47 percent to Lula's roughly 45 percent, defying polls that had Lula in front. Neither cleared the 50 percent needed to avoid a runoff. About 159 million people were eligible to vote, and the campaigns fought the final stretch over the cost of living, public security and corruption, with Lula warning that Washington would try to tilt the race toward Bolsonaro.

Brazil is Latin America's largest country and economy, so the result will shape the region's politics and its relationship with the United States. A Bolsonaro win would extend a rightward trend in parts of Latin America and restore his family to the presidency; a Lula win would keep a major progressive government in place and give him a fourth, nonconsecutive term.

Brazil's electronic voting usually produces a clear picture within hours of polls closing at 5 p.m. Brasília time. Watch the Superior Electoral Court count through the evening — and whether the early Lula lead holds as the big states report.
items.source: Poliwave / Superior Electoral Court live count

items.title: Trump rules out a Sunday strike on Iran, but keeps the threat on the table
items.summary:
President Trump said on Sunday there would be no U.S. strike on Iran that day, walking back — for 24 hours at least — his Saturday remark that a new attack could come 'maybe tomorrow.' He did not rule out action later, and he continued to frame the choice as binary: either Tehran reaches what he called a 'big, beautiful' agreement, or the United States resumes military operations.

Trump said his goal is to make sure Iran can never develop a nuclear weapon, and argued the earlier B-2 bomber operation was not enough to guarantee that outcome permanently. He also questioned whether Iran would honor any deal it signed. Iranian officials answered with warnings against miscalculation, as the conflict that began in February remains unresolved despite a ceasefire and unfinished peace talks.

The mixed signals matter well beyond the region. Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping routes all sit inside the blast radius of a renewed campaign, and markets head into a week already loaded with a Federal Reserve decision and major earnings with one more source of volatility on top.

Watch for any change in U.S. force posture in the Arabian Sea, fresh statements from Tehran, and whether indirect diplomatic messaging produces an actual proposal in the coming days.

items.title: France counts nearly 1,000 arrests after a second weekend of cost-of-living protests
items.summary:
French police arrested nearly 1,000 people on Saturday as cost-of-living demonstrations swept Paris and other cities for a second straight weekend. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said officers faced an extremely elevated level of violence from black-clad extremists on the fringes of the marches, and riot police fired tear gas in the capital as well as Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes. Two people were seriously injured, including a man in Toulouse who reportedly lost fingers.

Authorities deployed about 70,000 security personnel nationwide. Turnout estimates ranged from about 410,000 by the interior ministry to roughly 800,000 by the organizing CGT union, with the main Paris march drawing between 110,000 and 250,000 people. Nunez said the day ended better than the previous weekend, when rioting left public buildings vandalized, hundreds of shops looted and about 2,700 people arrested.

The unrest lands six months before France chooses a successor to President Emmanuel Macron, who is finishing 10 years in office and cannot run again. Anger over prices is colliding with anger over the crackdown itself, which critics call an assault on the right to protest — a combination that is reshaping the opening phase of the presidential race.

Courts have been jailing people from last weekend's riots in expedited hearings. Watch whether the unions call a third weekend of marches, and how the presidential candidates position themselves on both prices and policing.

items.title: Thousands protest in Prague over the government's public media overhaul
items.summary:
Thousands of people filled Prague's Old Town Square on Sunday to protest the Czech government's plan to overhaul how public television and radio are funded. The demonstration followed a rare overnight parliamentary vote in which government lawmakers gave initial backing to the changes outside the planned order of business, with debate limited and the vote held at about 4:36 a.m. on Saturday.

The proposal would abolish the household fees that currently fund Czech Television and Czech Radio and move their funding into the state budget. Critics, including media advocacy groups, say that would leave the broadcasters exposed to political pressure from whichever government holds the purse strings. Prime Minister Andrej Babis and his populist government, backed by the far-right SPD, say the change is about funding transparency, not an attack on independence.

Public media funding has become one of the defining fights of the Babis government, which has clashed repeatedly with both public and private outlets. Protest leaders told the crowd the government had 'gone too far,' and organizers say more demonstrations are planned while the bill sits in committee.

The bill still needs a later vote to become law. Watch the committee stage, the size of the next protests, and whether the government offers any independence safeguards to defuse the fight.

items.title: Russia fires 153 drones at Ukraine overnight, killing 8 and wounding 51
items.summary:
Russia launched another large overnight barrage at Ukraine, with Ukrainian officials saying eight people were killed and 51 were injured across the country over the past day. A drone hit a residential building in Vinnytsia, and in the Dnipro region a strike on an apartment building killed three people, including injuries to an 11-year-old girl in related attacks described by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

  Ukraine's air force put the wave at 153 Shahed-type drones, 92 of them jet-powered versions that fly faster and are harder to shoot down, plus low-cost cruise missiles. Other reporting from Kyiv said air defenses downed or suppressed 119 of the drones. Ukraine said it struck back at industrial and military sites inside Russia and in occupied Crimea, while Russian officials reported casualties in the Belgorod border region — figures from both sides that have not been independently verified.

  The pattern is a cold-weather campaign against power and heating infrastructure as temperatures fall, now in its fourth week. Zelenskyy used the attacks to press partners again to unblock Patriot interceptors and other air-defense help already approved in Europe, arguing that support cannot slow down just because talks are restarting.

  A narrow bright spot is separate from the barrage: Kyiv and Moscow have agreed to a localized pause around the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region to let aid in and civilians out, scheduled to begin in the coming days. Watch whether that pause actually holds and whether the next drone wave gets larger.
items.source: Kyiv Independent / Reuters via America Strikes

items.title: Trump rallies Port Huron with Rogers, James — and a surprise Nicki Minaj appearance
items.summary:
President Trump headlined a midterm rally Sunday afternoon at McMorran Place Arena in Port Huron, the first visit by a sitting president to the city. He brought Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Rep. John James back to the stage to urge turnout for the November 3 election, endorsed several other Michigan Republicans, and then surprised the crowd by bringing out rapper Nicki Minaj, who led a 'We love Trump' chant and called the moment a turning point for Michigan.

The rally was the Republican answer to former President Barack Obama's Detroit appearance on Saturday for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers' opponent in the open-seat Senate race. That contest — to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters — is one of the most expensive in the country and could decide Senate control, with Republicans defending a narrow 53-47 majority and Democrats needing a net gain of four seats in both chambers.

Michigan's auto tariff fight ran through the day as well. Rogers praised Trump's tariffs for drawing manufacturing investment while conceding the Canadian auto portion 'worries me a little bit' — a small but notable distance from the president in a state where the Detroit auto industry feels the trade standoff directly.

Early voting is already under way in Michigan. Watch turnout figures this week and whether either party's celebrity-powered weekend moves the Senate race's final polls.

items.title: Obama's Cleveland rally for Brown and Acton draws the midterm battle lines in Ohio
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama campaigned at Cleveland Public Auditorium on Saturday with Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, his first trip to Ohio since 2018. Speaking to thousands, he framed the November 3 vote as a chance for Ohioans to reject a Congress and governors he described as enabling the Trump administration.

  Obama blamed President Donald Trump for higher costs and attacked his immigration and foreign policy, while portraying Senator Jon Husted as a loyal vote for the administration and Vivek Ramaswamy as an opportunist. He also sharply condemned a Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's estranged mother, saying no office is worth that kind of tactic. Ramaswamy has kept the ad up despite a call from Governor Mike DeWine to remove it, and Husted's campaign answered that Obama and Brown together should worry Ohio voters.

  Both Ohio races remain tight and could matter nationally. Brown's race could help decide Senate control, and Acton is trying to put a Democrat in the governor's office for the first time since 2011. Democrats see an opening as Trump's approval falls and gas and grocery prices stay high, in a state Republicans have dominated in recent cycles.

  Obama also rallied in Detroit the same day for Michigan Democrats. Watch whether his weekend swing moves early-voting turnout in Cleveland and other Democratic strongholds in the final week.

items.title: Justice Department sues to hold up Alaska's Senate result if the Republican loses
items.summary:
The Justice Department filed suit on October 22 asking a federal court to stop Alaska from certifying its Senate election if Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan loses, pending an investigation into whether voters confused him with another candidate on the ballot, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan. President Trump told reporters on October 23 that he personally directed the department to file it.

  The department argues the second Sullivan's candidacy was meant to mislead, pointing to a similar campaign website and a history of supporting Democrats, and says a result affected by that confusion would violate federal voting law. State election officials had earlier reached a similar conclusion about a lack of good-faith candidacy, but Alaska's Supreme Court allowed the candidate to stay on the ballot, and he is running without a party affiliation.

  Democrat Mary Peltola, who is challenging the senator and leading in recent polling averages, called the suit a desperate and corrupt attempt to overturn an election, and her campaign promised to fight it. Election-law experts quoted in coverage called the federal argument exceptionally weak and noted that challenges to results normally come after votes are counted, not before.

  The case matters far beyond Alaska because it tests whether the federal government can intervene in a state's certification process in advance, in a race that could affect Senate control. Alaska also uses ranked-choice voting, which complicates any claim about where the second Sullivan's votes would have gone.

items.title: Nine days out, forecasts favor Democrats for the House and leave the Senate on a knife edge
items.summary:
Updated forecasts and prediction markets on October 25 agree on the broad shape of the midterms: Democrats are heavily favored to take the House, while Senate control is much closer. Traders put Democrats at about 91 to 92 percent to win the House and about 68 to 69 percent to win the Senate, while one independent forecast put the chances at 85 in 100 for the House and 55 in 100 for the Senate.

  The Senate math explains the gap. Republicans hold 53 seats, so Democrats need a net gain of four for an outright majority. The Cook Political Report sees Democratic gains of two to six seats and rates seven races as toss-ups, six of them in Republican-held seats in states including Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas, with Michigan the main Democratic seat in that group.

  National polling backs up the House picture, with Democrats leading the generic congressional ballot by about eight points in the RealClearPolling average and Cook projecting a Democratic gain of nine to 19 House seats. Individual Senate polling averages remain within a few points in almost every toss-up state, which is why markets and forecasters diverge most there.

  What to watch in the final week is whether late polls break consistently in one direction in those seven states, and whether early-voting turnout — running well ahead of 2022 in several battlegrounds — changes the picture forecasters are working from.

items.title: Ohio markets swing toward Acton and Brown as the governor's race reprices
items.summary:
Prediction markets for Ohio's two big races moved noticeably in the latest update, especially for governor. Amy Acton gained about eight points on Polymarket while Vivek Ramaswamy lost about seven, leaving Acton priced near 79 cents there and 77 cents on Kalshi. Combined boards for a party sweep of both Ohio races shifted in the same direction, with a Republican sweep falling sharply.

  The Senate race was calmer but still leans Democratic in the markets. Sherrod Brown was priced at about 64 to 66 percent to beat Senator Jon Husted, little changed from the prior update. Polling spreads for that race are wider, ranging from a Marist survey showing Brown ahead 51 to 43 to another pollster showing a near tie, and forecasters still rate it a toss-up.

  Traders and poll watchers say the next round of Ohio surveys is the most likely trigger for another move, along with turnout since early voting began on October 6. Brown has made data-center tax breaks a central attack, tying Husted to $2.5 billion in breaks from his time as lieutenant governor while residential electric bills have climbed, an issue Republican strategists themselves have flagged as a drag on Husted.

  The gap between market confidence in Brown and the tighter polling is the story to watch: markets are weighting his three past statewide Senate wins heavily, while forecasters are weighting how Republican Ohio has become since then.

items.title: Supreme Court lets New Hampshire enforce its ban on student IDs for voting
items.summary:
The Supreme Court ruled on October 22 that New Hampshire can fully enforce its ban on using student identification to vote in next month's election, pausing a lower-court order that would have let poll workers consider student IDs case by case when a voter has no government-issued ID. The brief, unsigned order pointed to the court's usual reluctance to change election rules close to a vote.

  The state, backed by Republican officials, argued the lower court's October 2 order created confusion about procedures less than three weeks before Election Day and misread state law. The voting-rights group challenging the ban argued the state had not shown any security problem specific to student cards, and the trial judge had found the change already kept at least one student from voting and could affect more young voters who lack other accepted ID.

  Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to dissent publicly, arguing the trial judge had not changed the rules but had corrected the secretary of state's reading of them, and that accurate information for voters matters especially with an election looming.

  New Hampshire's Senate race is one of the contests that will decide control of the chamber, so even a narrow ID rule can matter in a close count. The underlying lawsuit over whether the ban burdens young voters will continue after the election, but the ban will be in force on November 3.

items.title: The busiest week of earnings season collides with a Fed decision
items.summary:
About a third of the S&P 500 reports results this week, the peak of third-quarter earnings season, and the calendar stacks the biggest names on top of a Federal Reserve decision. Verizon opens the week Monday, Boeing, Coca-Cola and Visa follow Tuesday, and Alphabet, Microsoft, Ford and GE Vernova report Wednesday — hours after the FOMC announces its rate decision at 2 p.m. ET. Amazon, Caterpillar, Eli Lilly, Intel and Mastercard land Thursday, with ExxonMobil and Chevron closing the week Friday.

Markets expect the Fed to hold the federal funds rate steady — it raised the range to 3.75 to 4.00 percent in September — but futures put roughly 80 percent odds on another hike in December, which makes Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference the real event. Thursday also brings the advance estimate of third-quarter GDP, forecast near 3.2 percent, and September PCE inflation, expected to show the headline rate rising toward 3.7 percent.

Stocks go in wobbly: the S&P 500 slipped about half a percent last week and the Nasdaq about 0.7 percent, with chip stocks down more than 3 percent after disappointing prints from Meta and Lam Research. The hyperscalers' AI spending — heading toward roughly $800 billion this year — is the number investors will grade hardest.

Wednesday afternoon is the hinge: Fed statement, Warsh press conference, then Alphabet and Microsoft after the close. A hawkish surprise in any of the three could set the tone for the rest of the fall.

items.title: Samsung and SK hynix face a huge memory earnings test this week
items.summary:
Two South Korean chipmakers head into the most closely watched memory earnings of the year. SK hynix reports Wednesday, October 28, and Samsung reports Thursday, October 29, with market estimates putting their combined third-quarter operating profit near 185 trillion won, roughly $139.4 billion.

Samsung has already previewed the scale, guiding earlier in October to about 195 trillion won in revenue and about 107.4 trillion won in operating profit for the quarter. The driver is straightforward: prices for memory are climbing and demand is especially intense for high-bandwidth memory, the stacked, fast memory that sits next to AI processors in data centers.

Memory matters because AI systems cannot run on processors alone — they need data fed to them extremely quickly, and new factories take years to build, so supply stays tight when demand jumps. That scarcity is what turns higher prices into outsized profits for the few firms that can deliver advanced memory at scale.

The forward question is bigger than one quarter. Investors want to hear whether both companies can supply the next generation, HBM4, in volume for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform. A confident answer would support the idea that the boom has further to run; any hint of delay would raise doubts about how long current prices can hold, including for U.S. peer Micron and for Sandisk, which also reports this week.

items.title: Cerebras shows how it runs a 3-trillion-parameter AI model across 59 wafers
items.summary:
Cerebras published a technical explanation on Sunday of how it serves a 3-trillion-parameter version of Moonshot's Kimi model across 59 of its wafer-scale chips. The setup links the wafers with pipeline parallelism, uses compressed weights and cache formats, and is described as delivering roughly 1,000 to 2,000 or more tokens per second.

The same daily roundup noted a second, very different route to strong results: a small open-source project that coordinates five Qwen models through shared files and assigned roles, including a checker, scored on a hard coding benchmark at a level comparable to a leading frontier model. Commenters in both cases urged caution — the Cerebras system described is not the same as what public users can access today, and the multi-model coding result used an agentic loop on a benchmark designed for single attempts.

Together the two items capture where AI competition is moving. Chinese open models keep closing capability gaps, American hardware firms are experimenting with architectures far larger than a single conventional chip, and software coordination is squeezing more performance out of smaller, cheaper models that people can run on their own hardware.

Why it matters for business is cost and control. If smaller models working together, or specialized hardware running huge models very fast, can match frontier results more cheaply, pricing pressure on the big labs grows. Apollo's chief economist, cited in the same roundup, argues there is still no measurable productivity payoff outside tech — a reminder that technical feats and broad economic returns are not yet the same thing.

items.title: Walmart welcomes AI shopping agents while Amazon blocks them
items.summary:
Walmart is building a formal front door for AI agents to shop on a customer's behalf, at the same time Amazon has been blocking outside agents from completing purchases. Walmart's plan, announced October 21 and still rolling out into November, centers on an Agent Gateway for Walmart and Sam's Club.

Through that gateway, approved agents can look through inventory and place orders without the shopper handing over personal history or payment details directly to the agent. Each agent gets its own profile tied to the customer's account, so its orders show up separately. Shoppers can require approval for every purchase or set a spending limit, and they can delete the profile at any time — no Walmart+ membership required.

Walmart already connects with assistants including ChatGPT, Gemini and Meta's Muse, and its chief executive framed the move as preparing for shopping at scale by software, not just by people browsing pages. The company also set rules: agents must stay within the shopper's stated intent, see only the data a task needs, never touch card details, and face being cut off if they break the terms, with normal returns still applying.

The split between the two retail giants is about who owns the customer relationship. Opening up on its own terms gives Walmart a chance to be the store an AI chooses, even when the human never visits Walmart's site. Blocking agents protects Amazon's own browsing, advertising and assistant model. Which bet pays off will shape how online shopping works as agents become common.

items.title: Audi will build its first U.S. factory in Georgia, a $4 billion bet
items.summary:
Audi plans to build its first-ever factory in the United States, in the Macon, Georgia area, President Trump announced Saturday at a campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, with Audi's chief executive joining him on stage. Audi said the plant will create about 4,500 jobs and be designed for up to 200,000 vehicles a year, focused on its largest premium SUVs. The company put the investment at about $4 billion; Trump described it as $4.2 billion.

Production is not imminent. Audi said output is slated for the early 2030s, after construction in the coming years, reflecting how long a new auto plant and its supplier network take to build. The site choice was pitched on Georgia's ready industrial land, skilled workforce, existing auto supplier base and logistics.

For Audi the logic is defensive as well as growth-driven. It is the only major German luxury brand without U.S. production, building most U.S.-market vehicles in Germany, Mexico and Central and Eastern Europe, which left it exposed when tariffs rose. The company has said tariffs cost it about 1.2 billion euros in profit in 2025, with a similar hit expected this year, while its U.S. sales fell 16% last year to about 165,000 vehicles and sales in China dropped sharply.

Politically, the announcement landed in a battleground state days before the November 3 midterms, giving the administration a manufacturing win to campaign on in Georgia's Senate and governor races. Economically, the test will be years away — whether local production can restore Audi's competitiveness in its second-largest premium market without the tariff drag.

items.title: No deaths in the Florida A&M homecoming shooting; police hunt a single suspected shooter
items.summary:
Tallahassee police said Sunday that no one has died in Saturday night's shooting near Florida A&M University's Bragg Memorial Stadium, and that investigators now believe a single shooter fired into the homecoming crowd. Twelve people were hurt in all — 11 by gunfire, including six juveniles, the youngest 11 — and one victim's grandmother was injured fleeing. By Sunday, five victims had been released from the hospital, six remained hospitalized and one was in critical condition.

Police Chief Lawrence Revell said detectives from the Violent Crimes Unit reviewed digital evidence overnight and kept canvassing the Perry Street area on Sunday. The department opened a tip hotline at 850-891-4610 and an online portal for photos and video, with anonymous tips going to Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS. No arrest has been made and police say they do not yet have a person of interest.

The shooting followed the university's homecoming football game and has shadowed one of the biggest weekends on the FAMU calendar, which draws students, alumni and families from across the region. The university has stressed the gunfire happened near campus and that the campus itself remained safe.

'We need our community's help,' Revell said. Watch for the first identification of a suspect — the volume of phone video from a homecoming crowd makes witness evidence the most likely break in the case.
items.source: Tallahassee Police Department via Bazaar Daily News

items.title: World Series shifts to St. Petersburg with the Brewers two wins from a first title
items.summary:
The World Series moves to Tropicana Field on Monday night for Game 3, with the Milwaukee Brewers leading the Tampa Bay Rays 2-0 after a pair of one-run wins in Milwaukee — 3-2 in Game 1 and a 5-4 comeback from 4-0 down in Game 2. First pitch is 8 p.m. ET on FOX. Both franchises are chasing the first championship in their history.

Game 3 sets up the series' best pitching storyline: Rays starter Freddy Peralta, the ALCS MVP, faces the team he spent most of his career with. Peralta has been dominant since arriving in Tampa at the trade deadline, but his one start against Milwaukee this year — during a brief Mets stint in July — was a rough one, with seven earned runs in 5.1 innings. Robert Gasser is scheduled to start for Milwaukee.

Tampa Bay is not in must-win territory on paper, but practically it is close: coming back from 3-0 down has happened once in World Series history. The Rays also get their first World Series home game since 2008 — their 2020 appearance was played in the COVID bubble.

Games 4 and 5 follow Tuesday and Wednesday in St. Petersburg, with Games 6 and 7, if needed, back in Milwaukee on Friday and Saturday.

items.title: Trump and Obama trade Michigan weekends as early voting runs ahead of the midterms
items.summary:
Michigan got the full midterm treatment this weekend: former President Barack Obama rallied Detroit Democrats on Saturday for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, and President Trump answered Sunday in Port Huron for Republican Mike Rogers. Obama framed attacks on El-Sayed as an attempt to make him look less American, comparing it to the false claims he once faced about his own birthplace: 'We have seen this movie before. I starred in it.'

Trump dismissed Obama's efforts in an early Sunday Truth Social post before taking the stage in an area he carried with more than 66 percent of the vote in 2024. The open Senate seat — Gary Peters is retiring — is among the most closely watched and expensive races in the country, and both parties treat Michigan as a bellwether for the November 3 midterms.

The trade fight with Canada hangs over the state's politics, because the Detroit-based auto industry sits on the front line of the tariff standoff. Rogers has tried to hold both ends of that rope, crediting tariffs with manufacturing wins while voicing concern about the auto-specific levies.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the Senate and the House to flip Congress. Watch Michigan's early-vote totals this week for the first hard evidence of which side's weekend worked.

items.title: NFL Week 7 Sunday starts in Paris, ends with Chiefs at Seahawks
items.summary:
Week 7 of the NFL season opened Sunday morning with history: the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints played the league's first regular-season game at Stade de France in Saint-Denis, outside Paris, kicking off at 9:30 a.m. ET. Pittsburgh entered 4-2 and New Orleans 2-4.

The early afternoon window brought seven games at 1 p.m., including the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers at Atlanta, Cleveland at Tennessee, Cincinnati at Baltimore, and Indianapolis at the unbeaten Minnesota Vikings. The late window featured Denver at Arizona, Green Bay at Detroit and the Los Angeles Rams at Las Vegas.

Sunday night closes with the biggest matchup of the day: the unbeaten Kansas City Chiefs at the Seattle Seahawks, the defending Super Bowl champions, at 8:20 p.m. on NBC. Four teams — Buffalo, Jacksonville, the Los Angeles Chargers and Washington — are on bye this week.

For Ohio viewers, Cleveland's trip to Tennessee is the local draw, while the Bengals-Ravens divisional game carries direct AFC North implications alongside the Steelers' Paris game. Monday night then finishes the week with Dallas at Philadelphia.

items.title: Six Flags will add seat belts to Goliath after a rider fell to his death
items.summary:
Six Flags says it will add seat belts to its Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia and to other coasters that use a similar restraint system, following the death of a rider earlier this month. Goliath remains closed while safety reviews and official clearances continue.

The victim, 42-year-old Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, fell from the ride on October 12. Police said preliminary witness accounts indicated he was ejected, struck other riders and was found unresponsive beneath the coaster. Four minors were among several other parkgoers injured. Kariem was described by the company as a cherished member of a local public charter school community.

Goliath is a roughly 3.5-minute ride that reaches about 70 mph and 200 feet, using a waist lap-bar style restraint rather than an over-the-shoulder harness. Six Flags President and CEO John Reilly said the company has brought in independent engineers and ride inspection specialists to review procedures across its parks, and Goliath plus eight other rides at five additional parks remain temporarily closed out of caution, while more than 220 coasters across the company continue operating.

Georgia authorities and Cobb County police are still investigating what happened, including whether state safety requirements were followed. The coaster's most recent annual state inspection in March reported no violations, though a separate inspection this year noted bushings that needed replacement. What to watch is the investigation's findings and whether seat-belt retrofits become a broader standard for similar lap-bar coasters nationally.

items.title: Browns stun the Titans 27-24 on Szmyt's walk-off kick after trailing 14-0
items.summary:
The Browns did it the hard way again. Down 14-0 in the first quarter in Nashville, Cleveland clawed back to beat the Tennessee Titans 27-24 on Andre Szmyt's 32-yard field goal as time expired — their third walk-off win of the season and their second straight week decided by a kick at the gun. The win lifts Cleveland to 5-2 and keeps it in first place in the AFC North; Tennessee fell to 1-6.

Tony Pollard torched Cleveland early with touchdown runs of 36 and 10 yards, but Quinshon Judkins answered with two short scoring runs and Szmyt's 28-yarder at the halftime gun put the Browns ahead 17-14. After a scoreless third quarter, the teams traded blows: a Joey Slye field goal tied it, Deshaun Watson ran in from 9 yards, and Pollard's third touchdown, from the 1 with 58 seconds left, tied it again at 24. Watson then drove Cleveland 55 yards in four plays to set up the winner. Watson finished 25 of 36 for 308 yards — his first 300-yard game as a Brown — plus the rushing score, and rookie KC Concepcion caught 8 passes for 129 yards, all in the first half.

Cleveland outgained Tennessee 491 to 322 but needed a goal-line stand and every one of those yards to survive. Five of the Browns' seven games have now come down to a fourth-quarter go-ahead drive, which is thrilling and completely unsustainable — and, for now, winning football.

Next up is the division's heavyweight bout: Cleveland travels to Pittsburgh to face the 5-2 Steelers, with first place in the AFC North on the line.

items.title: Cavs survive another late collapse to beat Brooklyn in the home opener
items.summary:
Cleveland picked up its first win of the season on Saturday night at Rocket Arena, beating Brooklyn 125-121 in the home opener. Donovan Mitchell scored 22 points, and Jarrett Allen and Evan Mobley combined for 41 points, 18 rebounds and four blocks as the Cavaliers built a comfortable lead by halftime and pushed it to 22 points in the fourth quarter.

The finish was far tighter than it needed to be. Brooklyn rallied behind a hot fourth quarter, cutting a two-point margin in the final seconds after Michael Porter Jr. hit a late three. Porter then fouled Sam Merrill, whose two free throws pushed the lead back to four and closed out the win. The Nets also lost Day'Ron Sharpe to an ejection after a second flagrant foul on James Harden.

The pattern is the concern for Cleveland. For the second game in a row, the Cavaliers let a large second-half lead shrink late, and head coach Kenny Atkinson pointed afterward to turnovers, rebounding and late-game execution as areas that have to improve. The win counts, but it did not settle the closing questions.

Cleveland has little time to dwell on it. Minnesota visits Rocket Arena on Monday at 7 p.m., the first game in a demanding early stretch that also includes Oklahoma City, Philadelphia and New York in the coming weeks.

items.title: Plain Dealer breaks its own no-endorsement rule to back Acton for governor
items.summary:
The Plain Dealer and Cleveland.com editorial board reversed themselves on Sunday, ending a self-imposed policy of not endorsing in Ohio's governor and Senate races to endorse Democrat Amy Acton for governor. The board wrote that Acton had earned consideration on her record, preparation and commitment, and that she has 'kept showing up' across Ohio — while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, it said, 'has offered Ohioans far less reason to trust him.'

The editorial was unusually blunt about its trigger: a Ramaswamy campaign advertisement built around the estranged mother of Acton, who suffered sexual abuse as a child. The board called the ad 'vile' and wrote that using childhood sexual abuse as a weapon against the person who endured it crosses a line Ohioans should defend whatever their party. Ramaswamy has since shortened the ad, and Gov. Mike DeWine was among the Republicans who called for it to come down.

The endorsement lands nine days before Election Day in a race the Cook Political Report just moved from Toss Up to Lean Democrat, with a recent Bowling Green State University poll showing Acton ahead 50-44. The Columbus Dispatch and Akron Beacon Journal editorial boards have also endorsed Acton in the past week.

Newspaper endorsements rarely move races on their own anymore — but a board publicly breaking its own neutrality rule is a signal of how the ad fight has reframed the race's final week. Watch the next public polls and whether Ramaswamy's bus tour can change the subject.
items.source: The Plain Dealer / Cleveland.com via Acton campaign release

items.title: No early voting in Ohio on Sunday — polls reopen Monday with longer hours
items.summary:
Ohio voters who were hoping to cast an early ballot on Sunday, Oct. 25 will find their county board of elections closed. The state schedule does not list a session for that Sunday. Early in-person voting resumes Monday, Oct. 26 from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., beginning the final, extended-hours week before the Nov. 3 election.

The rest of the week keeps getting busier. Voting runs Tuesday, Oct. 27 from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 p.m., then Wednesday through Friday, Oct. 28-30 from 7:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., Saturday, Oct. 31 from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and finally Sunday, Nov. 1 from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. There is no early voting on Monday, Nov. 2. Election Day itself is Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls open from 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

Two deadlines matter as much as the hours. Requests for an absentee ballot must be received by the county board by 8:30 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 27. A completed absentee ballot is a separate step — under current Ohio rules it must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day to count, so a postmark alone is not enough.

For Cuyahoga County and other northeast Ohio voters, the practical advice is to use Monday's long day rather than waiting for the final weekend, when lines at the single early-voting site in each county tend to be longest.

items.title: Ohio State heads to USC on Halloween still missing its quarterback
items.summary:
No. 3 Ohio State (6-1) comes off its bye week and travels to No. 16 USC (6-1) on Saturday, October 31, for a 7:30 p.m. ET kickoff on NBC at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum — and it will do so without starting quarterback Julian Sayin. Coach Ryan Day said Sayin, hurt when his throwing arm bent awkwardly on a sack at Indiana, is out indefinitely, and the program is planning as if he could miss the rest of the regular season and the postseason.

The job falls to a freshman competition between Luke Fahey, who replaced Sayin at Indiana, and former five-star Tavien St. Clair. Fahey, from Mission Viejo, California, would be making his first start in his home state. Whoever starts still gets to throw to Jeremiah Smith, who passed Braylon Edwards for the most receiving touchdowns by a Big Ten wideout in the Indiana win.

USC quarterback Jayden Maiava leads the Big Ten with 2,045 passing yards and 18 touchdowns, and the Trojans average 36.4 points a game — a stress test for an Ohio State defense that has carried the team. Oddsmakers still make the Buckeyes about a touchdown favorite, with one widely shared prediction landing at Ohio State 24, USC 21.

The game opens a brutal closing stretch: after USC, Ohio State hosts Oregon and Northwestern, then finishes at Nebraska and against Michigan. Saturday night will show whether the Buckeyes' playoff path survives its quarterback problem.

items.title: Guardians keep their dugout together after falling short in the ALCS
items.summary:
Cleveland will not be starting over this winter. After the Guardians' season ended in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series against Tampa Bay, manager Stephen Vogt made clear at the club's Oct. 22 wrap-up at Progressive Field that he is staying, and veteran pitching coach Carl Willis told the front office he wants to return as well.

Willis matters because pitching has been Cleveland's identity. Now approaching 66 and with the club since 2018, he has overseen staffs that have finished with an earned run average under 4.00 in eight seasons. Cleveland posted a 3.77 ERA in 2026, following 3.70 in 2025 and 3.61 in 2024, and the front office views that continuity as central to staying competitive without a large payroll.

The same week brought an individual honor for a pitcher who barely appeared in October. Tanner Bibee, Cleveland's opening day starter, won his second Fielding Bible Award for his defense during the regular season, even though he threw only a third of an inning in the postseason and did not pitch at all in the ALCS — a usage decision Vogt explained as holding him for a long extra-innings role that never came up.

For fans, the message heading into the offseason is stability at the top and a familiar question underneath it. Keeping Vogt and Willis preserves the pitching foundation, but the ALCS showed an offense that scored three runs or fewer in five straight games. What Cleveland adds at the plate this winter will decide whether that stability turns into another deep run.

baby.fact: Your baby already knows your voices. Babies in the womb hear sounds from the outside world in the third trimester, and newborns reliably turn toward their mother's voice within hours of birth — all that talking and reading to the bump has been registering.
